keyFacts: Landlord leased basement/ground-floor commercial space to tenant for a five-year term as sales offices. Recurring flooding after every rainstorm (one incident dropped roughly five inches of water during a business meeting) made the space unusable, and the landlord did nothing to fix it despite repeated complaints.
outcome: Judgment for the tenant. The New Jersey Supreme Court held the tenant was constructively evicted and relieved of liability for rent for the balance of the term (roughly 2.25 years remaining on the lease).
notes: Landmark, widely cited constructive-eviction case establishing that recurring flooding the landlord fails to remedy breaches quiet enjoyment. Opinion does not state a specific dollar recovery for the tenant beyond relief from unpaid rent; treat as a principle-establishing case.

caseName: Barash v. Pennsylvania Terminal Real Estate Corp.
keyFacts: Attorney-tenant leased office space in a sealed, air-conditioned high-rise; the lease only obligated the landlord to provide air conditioning during limited business hours. After hours, air flow stopped and the landlord offered after-hours ventilation only for a $25/hour fee. Tenant did not vacate but sued for breach.
outcome: Judgment for the landlord. The Court of Appeals held there was no actual or constructive eviction because the landlord did not fail to provide anything actually required by the lease, and, separately, that a tenant who remains in possession cannot claim constructive eviction.
notes: Negative/defense-side outcome. Useful as a principle case: (1) constructive eviction requires abandonment, and (2) landlord conduct must breach an actual lease obligation, not merely a pre-lease representation negated by a merger clause.

caseName: Fifth Avenue Building Co. v. Kernochan
keyFacts: Commercial tenant leased first-floor and basement space including a vault under the adjoining sidewalk. The City revoked the vault license and built a wall cutting the tenant off from that space to build a subway line; the tenant was wholly excluded from the vault for roughly two years and partially thereafter.
outcome: Judgment for the tenant (opinion by Judge Cardozo). Held that this was an actual (not merely constructive), if partial, eviction by act attributable to conduct the landlord permitted, and that a landlord may not apportion rent after evicting a tenant from any part of the demised premises — the entire rent was suspended during the exclusion.
notes: Old but foundational precedent (still cited) on the actual-vs-constructive eviction distinction and on partial interference with possession suspending rent. No modern dollar figure available; principle-only.

caseName: Charles E. Burt, Inc. v. Seven Grand Corp.
keyFacts: Commercial tenant in an office building was denied heat, electricity, and elevator service by the landlord from November 1957 to May 1958, essential services the lease obligated the landlord to supply.
outcome: Judgment for the tenant. The SJC held the landlord's failure to provide vital services was a material breach amounting to constructive eviction upon the tenant's abandonment, excusing further rent, with damages assessed for the affected period (found to be nearly equal to the rent for that period).
dollarAmountBasis: Damages described as approximately equal to rent for the roughly 6-month period of service failure, but no exact figure is stated in available summaries.
notes: Leading Massachusetts precedent on failure-to-provide-essential-services as constructive eviction. Exact dollar figure not confirmed from a primary source; treat dollar estimate as unverified.

keyFacts: Financial printing company leased commercial space; beginning in 1991 it repeatedly complained of roof leaks threatening equipment and inventory. The landlord made repeated but unsuccessful repair attempts, and the tenant eventually vacated by the end of 1991, having paid rent through the year.
outcome: Judgment for the tenant. The trial court (jury-waived) found constructive eviction; the SJC affirmed the result on a different theory (mutual dependence of lease covenants in commercial leases) and upheld an award of $1,063 in relocation damages for moving machinery and the telephone system, well below the tenant's claimed $14,000+ in moving costs.
dollarAmountBasis: Trial court's relocation-damages award for moving machinery and relocating the phone system, affirmed on appeal.
notes: Good illustration that even where liability is found, damages actually proven/awarded can be modest relative to what a tenant claims. Also established Massachusetts' 'dependent covenants' rule for commercial leases.

caseName: Automobile Supply Co. v. Scene-In-Action Corp.
keyFacts: Commercial office tenant was denied adequate heat for much of the winter of 1927-28 despite repeated complaints to the landlord. Tenant gave notice in February 1928 that it would vacate April 30, 1928, roughly five months before the lease's actual September 1928 expiration.
outcome: Judgment for the landlord. The trial court awarded the landlord five months' rent (May-September 1928); the Illinois Supreme Court's opinion is a leading statement of the rule that liability for rent continues so long as the tenant remains in possession, and articulates the reasonable-time-to-vacate requirement for a constructive eviction defense.
notes: Negative outcome for tenant. Frequently cited Illinois authority; useful as a principle case showing the timing risk of delaying abandonment after a repair failure.

caseName: Frittelli, Inc. v. 350 North Canon Drive, LP
court: California Court of Appeal, Second Appellate District, Division Four
keyFacts: Gourmet doughnut shop tenant in a Beverly Hills shopping center sued after the landlord's renovation of the center allegedly destroyed visibility to customers and let dust into the premises, claiming breach of quiet enjoyment and negligence.
outcome: Summary judgment for the landlord affirmed. The lease's remodeling clause (which allowed remodeling and limited landlord liability for related damages, subject only to a proportional rent abatement) modified the implied covenant of quiet enjoyment; the tenant's claims failed as a matter of law.
notes: Important cautionary/principle case: standard commercial lease remodeling and exculpatory clauses can waive or narrow the covenant of quiet enjoyment in California. No damages were awarded to the tenant.

court: California Court of Appeal, Second Appellate District
keyFacts: Retail tenant on La Brea Avenue in Los Angeles complained beginning in late 2003 of rainwater and wastewater leaking into the store, a floor indentation, peeling paint, and cockroaches, and demanded repairs. Tenant remained in possession and sued for breach of quiet enjoyment and related claims.
outcome: Mixed result on appeal. The court held that breach of the covenant of quiet enjoyment sounds in contract, not tort, when the tenant remains in possession and there is no actual or constructive eviction; punitive damages were unavailable absent a wrongful-eviction claim. A separate trial-court finding of a perpetual lease renewal was reversed.
notes: Useful principle case on the contract-vs-tort character of quiet enjoyment claims in California and the unavailability of punitive damages absent eviction. No specific compensatory dollar figure confirmed from available summaries.

caseName: K&S Enterprises v. Kennedy Office Supply Co., Inc.
court: North Carolina Court of Appeals, affirmed by North Carolina Supreme Court
keyFacts: Landlord failed to repair a badly leaking roof over commercial premises leased for use as a restaurant. The tenant claimed the disrepair rendered the space unfit for its intended restaurant use and vacated.
outcome: Judgment for the tenant. The Court of Appeals held the landlord's failure to repair the roof constituted constructive eviction, which under North Carolina law automatically operates as a breach of the implied covenant of quiet enjoyment; affirmed by the North Carolina Supreme Court.
notes: Leading North Carolina authority tying failure-to-repair directly to constructive eviction/quiet enjoyment. No specific damages figure found in available summaries.

caseName: Daftary v. Prestonwood Market Square, Ltd.
court: Court of Appeals of Texas, Dallas
keyFacts: Dental practice held over in its shopping-center space after lease expiration (paying holdover rent the landlord accepted) and repeatedly complained about disruptive noise from a neighboring dance studio also leasing from the same landlord, which the landlord failed to address.
outcome: Jury verdict for the tenant on constructive eviction was reinstated on appeal. The court held that constructive eviction can apply to a holdover tenancy and that thirteen months to relocate an established dental practice was reasonable (expert testimony put standard relocation time at 12-18 months); case remanded for further proceedings on the breach-of-warranty claim and remedy election.
notes: Texas precedent extending constructive eviction to holdover tenancies. Jury damages amount not confirmed from available secondary sources; case was remanded, so final damages figure may not be publicly reported.

caseName: Westwood Motorcars, LLC v. Virtuolotry, LLC
keyFacts: A commercial tenant sued its landlord and the landlord's manager for breach of contract and constructive eviction in district court after a separate justice-court eviction suit had already awarded the landlord possession; a jury found for the tenant and awarded damages in the district-court suit.
outcome: The court of appeals had reversed and rendered a take-nothing judgment against the tenant, reasoning the tenant's earlier concession to the justice-court possession judgment barred the damages suit. The Texas Supreme Court reversed, holding a justice-court possession judgment has no preclusive effect on a later district-court damages suit for constructive eviction, and remanded.
notes: Very recent (2024) Texas Supreme Court procedural ruling important for valuation purposes: confirms a tenant who loses/concedes a JP-court eviction (possession) suit is NOT thereby barred from later pursuing a district-court damages claim for constructive eviction. Jury's original damages figure from the underlying trial not stated in the appellate opinion summaries reviewed.

caseName: Katz Deli of Aventura, Inc. v. Waterways Plaza, LLC
court: Florida Third District Court of Appeal
keyFacts: Deli/restaurant tenant leased space in an Aventura shopping plaza starting in 2002. The roof began leaking in 2002 and worsened despite tenant complaints; the landlord made only minor, temporary repairs and refused to replace the roof, resulting in open water flows, mold, and odor that made the space unusable as a restaurant by May 2003. Tenant vacated in July 2003.
outcome: Judgment for the tenant. Trial court found the landlord grossly negligent in failing to maintain the roof and found constructive eviction/breach of lease; awarded the tenant prospective lost profits through the end of the lease's initial term (April 2007) but denied lost profits for renewal option years as too speculative. Court of Appeal affirmed both the liability finding and the damages measure/limitation on appeal and cross-appeal.
dollarAmountBasis: Trial court awarded prospective/future lost profits through April 2007 (end of initial 5-year lease term); exact dollar figure not confirmed in available secondary sources.
notes: Good Florida illustration of lost-profits as the damages measure for constructive eviction of a restaurant/food-service tenant, and of courts capping speculative future-profits claims at the original (not renewal) lease term.

caseName: Sears, Roebuck & Co. v. 69th Street Retail Mall, L.P.
keyFacts: Sears operated a department store at a Philadelphia-area shopping mall/retail complex under a legacy, below-market lease. After acquiring the property in 2005, the new landlord (seeking to replace Sears with a more lucrative tenant) allowed the property to deteriorate badly: falling façade brick, rodent infestation, sewage overflow and routine flooding, neglected landscaping, falling parking-garage debris, poor lighting, and open drug/prostitution activity in the garage, ultimately forcing Sears to vacate.
outcome: Judgment for the tenant. The Superior Court affirmed the landlord's liability for constructive eviction under a cumulative-interference or 'death by a thousand cuts' theory — i.e., no single defect was independently sufficient, but years of accumulated neglect together rendered the premises unsuitable for the leased purpose.
notes: Significant, widely-discussed Pennsylvania precedent recognizing a 'cumulative interference' theory of constructive eviction for large anchor-tenant leases. Specific jury/trial damages figure not confirmed from available secondary sources despite multiple search attempts (primary opinion PDF could not be parsed via automated fetch).

keyFacts: Landlord leased a one-story building to a tenant for a printing and photographic business, then began adding a second story while the tenant was in occupancy. Construction removed part of the roof, letting light into the tenant's darkroom, and generated dust and debris that contaminated the tenant's printing equipment; the landlord continued construction despite the tenant's protests and after a restraining order was dissolved.
outcome: Judgment for the tenant. The Colorado Supreme Court defined constructive eviction as any landlord disturbance of the tenant's possession that renders the premises unfit for their leased purpose or deprives the tenant of beneficial enjoyment, causing abandonment. The trial court's $2,212 judgment for the tenant was upheld and the landlord's counterclaim for remaining rent was dismissed.
dollarAmountBasis: Trial court judgment amount for the tenant, affirmed on appeal.
notes: Foundational Colorado constructive-eviction definition, arising from a landlord's active construction interference rather than mere disrepair — useful as an 'interference by landlord conduct' fact pattern.

caseName: DeBruyn Bros. Realty Co. v. Photo Lith Plate Service Corp.
keyFacts: Commercial tenant's leased premises suffered a rodent infestation and the landlord failed to provide required heat, conditions the tenant argued rendered the space unfit for its business purpose.
outcome: Judgment for the tenant. The Michigan Court of Appeals held the rodent infestation and failure to provide heat amounted to constructive eviction, relieving the tenant of further rent liability upon vacating.
notes: Cited in the Michigan judiciary's own landlord-tenant benchbook as a standard example of failure-to-repair/failure-to-maintain rising to constructive eviction. Full-text primary opinion was not independently retrieved; citation and facts drawn from secondary judicial-education source.

caseName: Sentry Water Systems, Inc. v. ADCA Corp.
court: Florida Second District Court of Appeal
keyFacts: Foundational Florida appellate case defining the elements a commercial tenant must prove to establish constructive eviction.
outcome: The court held that to establish constructive eviction under Florida law, a tenant must show 'wrongdoing' by the landlord — i.e., a wrongful, unwarranted, or unlawful act done with the express or implied intent to interfere with the tenant's beneficial enjoyment of the premises — and that the tenant abandoned the premises within a reasonable time after that act.
notes: Principle-only case (elements/standard), still cited by Florida courts including in Katz Deli. Facts of the underlying dispute were not confirmed beyond the legal holding; include for its precedential/standard-setting value rather than facts or damages.

caseName: Miami-Dade commercial tenant water-intrusion quiet enjoyment case (plaintiff/defendant names not disclosed in source)
citation: Miami-Dade County Court (Florida) bench trial verdict; case number and full case name not disclosed in the secondary source reviewed
keyFacts: A Miami-based healthcare company leased an entire penthouse floor of an office building for executive offices and a call center. After a significant tenant build-out, the space suffered recurring water intrusion; repeated remediation and ongoing construction activity disrupted the tenant's business operations over an extended period.
outcome: Judgment for the tenant after a multi-day bench trial. The court awarded $570,000 in damages plus entitlement to attorney's fees, finding the tenant proved sustained disruption, loss of use, and out-of-pocket mitigation expenses caused by the landlord's failure to remediate the water-intrusion conditions.
dollarAmountBasis: Court's damages award following bench trial, as reported by defense counsel's law-firm case summary (the tenant's own litigation counsel is not the source; this summary is from counsel representing the tenant/plaintiff per the firm's practice description).
notes: Real, specific dollar figure from a law firm's own case-result announcement rather than a published opinion; case name, docket number, and citation could not be independently verified/located. Treat as directionally reliable (law firms are subject to advertising-rules accuracy requirements) but not court-record-verified. Do not present as a citable published opinion.

caseName: Toxic mold commercial-lease settlement — SW Delray Artist Alley, LLC (plaintiff tenant name not disclosed in source)
citation: Settlement following appellate ruling; Florida (Delray Beach) — case name, docket number, and citation not disclosed in the secondary source reviewed
court: Florida state court (trial and appellate level not specified in source)
keyFacts: Commercial tenant in Delray Beach, Florida alleged its leased unit became uninhabitable due to toxic mold, asbestos, and volatile organic compounds (VOCs). Despite repeated complaints, the landlord (SW Delray Artist Alley, LLC) refused remediation; the tenant alleged resulting health issues and business interruption and ultimately vacated.
outcome: Tenant prevailed on appeal establishing landlord liability (breach of quiet enjoyment, breach of implied warranty of suitability, negligence, and breach of contract/security-deposit claims were asserted). The parties then settled for $435,000, covering business interruption/lost profits, medical treatment and personal injury damages, and relocation/restoration costs, shortly before a scheduled trial.
dollarAmountBasis: Settlement amount reported by plaintiff's counsel following an appellate liability ruling in the tenant's favor.
notes: Real dollar figure but from plaintiff's own law-firm marketing page rather than a published opinion or court record; case name/citation/docket could not be independently verified. A settlement, not a judgment — the $435,000 reflects negotiated resolution of multiple claims (including personal injury) bundled together, so it is not a clean 'quiet enjoyment damages' figure. Use with caution and do not present as a citable case.
